title: Work profile (BYOD)
text: Work profile (BYOD) Profile-owner mode manages only the work profile and leaves the personal side alone — company apps and data stay controlled while photos and messages stay private. The BYOD compromise, backed by Android Enterprise.

title: Fully managed (corporate)
text: Fully managed (corporate) Device-owner mode — usually via QR provisioning — grants full-device control including wipe and kiosk. A managed device shows its AE roots in the inventory: the EMM agent fields record the installation type. Where to find it Devices → click a Device ID → Network & EMM

title: Managed Google Play
text: Managed Google Play Alongside silent pushes and the private store, apps can be approved from Managed Google Play — Google's enterprise channel, curated by the admin. See the deployment paths in Apps →

title: Sync AE devices
text: Sync AE devices Google-side changes don't walk over by themselves: the Sync AE Devices toolbar action pulls the latest Android Enterprise inventory into FieldX. Run it after adding devices on the Google side. Where to find it Devices → inventory toolbar → Sync AE Devices

title: Reading the pills
text: Reading the pills Every restriction carries platform pills: green is FieldX EMM, orange is Android Enterprise , blue is Samsung. Some entries carry a version floor — the default-apps family, for example, needs Android Enterprise v16+.

title: AE-only entries
text: AE-only entries A few restrictions exist only on Android Enterprise — the credential-provider policies, for instance. The fastest way to find them all is the platform column of the master list. Where to find it Restrictions → Master Summary →

title: Push Apps list
text: Push Apps list Push Apps is the force-install channel: apps go to devices instead of waiting to be fetched. Entries push the moment they are saved and enabled; online units install at once, offline units catch up on reconnect. What it does Pushes an app to devices immediately after saving its details. Devices must be online to receive it; offline units get it once they come back online. List Search box + Add button; each row shows app Name, Package Name and a status dot; Rows-per-page pagination. Where to find it Apps → Push Apps

title: App detail
text: App detail The detail sheet is one app’s mission control: who gets it, which build, whether it is on, where it downloads from — and the installed ring showing live rollout progress across the assignment. Buttons Refresh re-reads state, Start Rollout begins deployment, Edit opens the editor, Delete removes the app. Enable flow New entries start Disabled — search the entry, click Enable (top-right), and a green dot marks it live; pushing begins for the assigned groups. Field Example Assigned Groups All devices (in this Zone) Zone Global Zone Version / Version Code 3.2.1 / 321 Package Name com.example.sales Enabled / Auto Update On / Off toggles Download Link Direct APK URL with copy button Last Updated / File size Date-time / size in MB Installed ring Live percentage of assigned devices with the app installed.

title: Split APK & XAPK packages
text: Split APK & XAPK packages Split packages exist because stores slim downloads per device configuration. FieldX sidesteps the store entirely, so it wants the raw APKs re-packed plainly — zips of zips and bundled folders will not install. Split APKs Generate the APKs, put them in one folder, and zip the folder contents — the ZIP must contain only APK files, no folders — then push the ZIP like any app. XAPK / APKM Rename to .zip, delete everything except the APK files, re-zip APKs only, and push. Not supported AAB format (Google Play) cannot be pushed.

title: Updating an app
text: Updating an app Updates are new builds of the same listing, not new listings. The platform guards this with signature matching, so a wrong-key APK can never silently replace a production app. 1. Increment the Version Code and sign with v1+v2 using the SAME keys as before. 2. Upload to your hosting, copy the link. 3. Push Apps → search the listing → Edit → replace the link → details pre-populate. Signatures must match If the signature hashes differ from the previous build, Save stays disabled. 4. Verify groups → Submit — devices update in a staggered rollout.

title: Deleting a listing
text: Deleting a listing A listing is the portal’s record of an app, not the app on devices. Deleting tidies the catalog; the installed copies stay until a restriction or action removes them — hence disable-before-delete. Push Apps → search → select the listing → Delete (top-right) → confirm. Prefer Disable Disabling beats deleting for cleanup-safe pauses; delete only to tidy the section. Important Deleting a listing does NOT uninstall the app from devices — add a “Force uninstall App” restriction for that.

title: Add via APK link
text: Add via APK link Adding starts with a link, not an upload. The portal fetches the APK, reads its metadata, and pre-fills the form — the admin’s job shifts from typing details to verifying them. 1. Paste a Download Link → Fetch App Details. Rules Enter a valid APK link that is directly downloadable. Google Drive and file-storage links are not supported — HTTPS only. See the Knowledge Base article for details. Signing Sign APKs with both v1 and v2 schemes, as Android recommends. Hosting Upload to your own web hosting (e.g. Amazon S3, GoDaddy). FieldX never hosts apps on the portal for security reasons; OneDrive, Google Drive and Dropbox links are not supported. Add dialog — paste a direct HTTPS APK link to fetch details.

title: Edit app
text: Edit app Editing is where deployment policy lives: what build, who gets it, when it may install, and whether it updates itself. Save re-targets the whole assignment in one move. Auto-filled metadata Package Name, Version, Version Code, File size, Min/Target SDK, Supported ABI — plus md5 / sha1 / sha256 Signatures for verification. Options App Name, Managed Config (+ Add/Update), Runtime Permissions (e.g. Prompt), Auto update from Google Play Store. Install window Install anytime of the day, or around a time (~60 min) with a Time picker. Targeting All devices (in this Zone), or Push only to selected groups with an Assigned Groups picker. Finish with Save.

title: Custom App Store
text: Custom App Store The private store flips distribution around: instead of pushing apps out, admins publish a shelf and users pull what they need. Same catalog mechanics underneath — groups decide who sees what. What it is The FieldX Store plugin — an internal, enterprise app store for devices with no Play Store. It is NOT preinstalled, so you choose exactly which devices or groups get it. Put the Store on devices Downloads → Plugin Apps → copy icon next to App Store → Push Apps → Add → paste the link → pre-populated details → pick Groups → Submit → open the entry → Enable (green dot = live) → auto-installs. Fill the Store Host APKs yourself (e.g. S3) → App Store page → Add → paste link to prefill → pick a Category (20 + Home, multi-select) → pick device groups → Save — entries appear for users to download. Why Groups Group targeting makes the Store flexible: different apps for different devices, regions or zones. Where to find it Apps → Custom App Store (tutorial in the Knowledge Base)

title: Managed Google Play
text: Managed Google Play Managed Play bridges the public store and fleet control: approve once from Google’s catalog, then distribute with FieldX targeting, configs and update modes. No sideloading, no APK hosting. What it does Pick an app from the Google Play store and push it to devices. Click the Google Play icon to load the embedded store, then select apps into your App Catalog. List has Search, Play shortcut and refresh. Detail extras Everything in Push Apps, plus the Play Store listing URL, Managed Config JSON (e.g. VPN or server settings), Auto Update Mode (e.g. Default low-priority), and Grant Runtime Permissions (for v4.1+). Buttons Edit, Start Rollout, Delete. Where to find it Apps → Managed Google Play

title: What is MDM?
text: What is MDM? Managing phones, tablets and other endpoints from a central console instead of touching each one. Enroll a device once; afterwards apps, settings, policies and updates go out over the air — to ten units or ten thousand. Every MDM product does three jobs: configure devices without handling them, secure company data on devices you don't fully own, and maintain fleets — updates, apps, health — at scale. Without MDM each change is manual labor per device; with it, one action covers the fleet.

title: UEM vs MDM vs EMM
text: UEM vs MDM vs EMM Overlapping names for the same idea at different widths. MDM (Mobile Device Management) covers phones and tablets. EMM (Enterprise Mobility Management) is Android-centered management with app and content controls. UEM (Unified Endpoint Management) stretches the idea to every endpoint — laptops, desktops, IoT. FieldX lives in the MDM/EMM space with UEM-style breadth: Android first, plus Apple and Linux fleets from the same console.

title: Ownership models
text: Ownership models Who owns the device decides how far your control may go. Corporate-owned units accept everything — lockdown, wipe, kiosk (think retail POS or warehouse scanners). BYOD — personal phones — gets partial control through a work profile that walls off company data without touching photos and messages. Shared devices — classrooms, nurse carts — optimize for fast handover and tamper resistance. Choose the model before writing a single policy; every later decision follows from it.

title: Management modes
text: Management modes On Android, control depth depends on how the device was provisioned. Device-owner mode (QR, Knox or ADB enrollment) grants full-device control including wipe and kiosk. Profile-owner mode manages only the work profile and leaves the personal side alone — the BYOD compromise. Samsung Knox adds hardware-backed extras on supported devices. The tradeoff is setup cost: stronger modes usually need a factory reset, weaker modes enroll with less friction.

title: The device lifecycle
text: The device lifecycle Every managed device travels the same loop. Enroll it once, by whichever method fits. It joins groups — manually or through auto-grouping rules — and inherits their policies. It then lives under monitoring , where dashboards, alerts and instant actions keep it healthy. Reports turn that history into proof for audits and SLAs. When its tour ends, it leaves cleanly : unenroll to release it, factory-reset to wipe it for the next user.

title: Console, agents, channel, server
text: Console, agents, channel, server Four moving parts. The console is the web portal where admins enroll devices, build groups, write restrictions and read reports. On-device agents (Manager, Updater, Kiosk, Store) enforce those decisions locally. A persistent channel carries commands instantly instead of waiting for check-ins. Behind it all, FieldX-hosted or private servers store inventory, policies and history.

title: What FieldX does differently
text: What FieldX does differently No Google dependency — enrollment, push and updates work without Play Services or Firebase, including de-Googled builds and blocked regions. Instant commands over a persistent connection instead of polling delays. Encrypted SMS fallback keeps lock, wipe and reboot working with zero data. CDN firmware delivery with staged rollout and rollback for custom builds.

title: A day with FieldX
text: A day with FieldX Morning: the dashboard shows overnight compliance and offline units. Midday: a new store batch enrolls by QR into its group and inherits policies automatically. Afternoon: a staged app update rolls to 10% while signage kiosks report uptime. Evening: scheduled reports land in inboxes. The pattern never changes: enroll once, target by group, verify by report.

title: How a policy reaches a device
text: How a policy reaches a device Follow one restriction from thought to enforcement. You write it once in the console and attach it to a group — never to individual devices. Where rules conflict, the priority order decides which wins. The console pushes it instantly over the persistent channel (or encrypted SMS if the device is offline), the on-device agent enforces it locally , and compliance shows up in Devices and Reports. Change the group, and every member follows.

title: Terms you will meet
text: Terms you will meet Group, Zone and Bucket organize devices at different levels. Restriction, Policy and Order control behavior with priority. Kiosk, OTA, Watchdog, Geofence and App Limits are the headline features. Hover any dotted term anywhere in these docs for its one-line definition.

title: Device inventory table
text: Device inventory table The inventory is the master list of every device FieldX manages. Each row is one endpoint with its identifiers, owner, freshness and hardware. Admins start here for daily fleet checks, rollout audits, and locating a single unit by IMEI or serial. What it does Lists every enrolled device with checkbox selection and columns for Device ID, IMEI Number, Serial Number, Device User, Alias, Last Seen Time, Model and Manufacturer. Toolbar Refresh icon re-reads the list; Sync AE Devices pulls the latest Android Enterprise inventory. Where to find it Devices (top-level console page) Inventory table — every enrolled demo unit with identifiers, freshness and hardware.

title: Bulk actions menu
text: Bulk actions menu Bulk actions apply one operation to many devices at once. Tick checkboxes, open the gear menu, and the command runs across the whole selection — moving zones, assigning groups, exporting records, or removing units. What it does The gear icon applies one operation to every selected device. Menu item Effect Change Zone Moves devices to another zone with its policies Assign Group Attaches devices to a group for policy targeting Assign User to device Links a device to a user Unassign User Releases the device from its user Export CSV Downloads the selected inventory rows Bulk enroll Devices Starts enrollment for a batch of units Delete Devices Removes units from management Archive Devices Archives units out of the active lists

title: Identity & status
text: Identity & status Identity fields never change for a device: its ID, IMEI, serial, model and OS version. Status fields change constantly: activation state, last-seen time, registration date and compliance posture. Together they answer two questions — which device is this, and is it healthy? Field Example Device ID DEMO-8F3K-2A91 IMEI Number 860000000000001 Serial Number DEMO-SN-0001 Model & Manufacturer Galaxy A14 / Samsung OS Version v13 (API 33) Zone / Groups Demo Zone / Demo-Retail Status Activated, Last Seen, Registration Date Compliance Keyguard, lock screen, security patch date, SELinux, bootloader state All values above are dummy data for illustration. Device Details tab — identity, status and compliance at a glance (identifiers redacted).

title: System & battery
text: System & battery System parameters show live resource pressure: CPU load, memory and storage fill, battery charge and temperature. Power and screen fields reveal how the device is actually used day to day. Check here first when a single device misbehaves. System CPU load and frequency, memory and storage usage with percentages, external storage, brightness. Battery Charge remaining, charger plugged-in time, voltage, health status, battery and CPU temperature. Power & screen Power-on time, power-save / idle / standby modes, resolution, size, orientation, ringer mode. Hardware Radio, bootloader and build numbers, build type, device fingerprint, supported ABI, default apps (Home, keyboard, SMS, dialer), locale and time zone.

title: Network & EMM
text: Network & EMM Network fields show how the device reaches the world: Wi-Fi network and address, cellular SIMs and roaming, Bluetooth peers, VPN state and location mode. The EMM fields describe the management agent itself — its version, installation type and resource use. Wi-Fi Connected SSID, IP and MAC address, total Wi-Fi data usage. Mobile Dual-SIM IMEIs, carrier, roaming status, mobile data usage per slot. More Bluetooth MAC and connected devices, VPN service and active state, location mode and last update, connectivity log. EMM agent Manager version, installation type (e.g. AE), app memory used/available, app UID.

title: Installed Apps
text: Installed Apps The installed-apps table is the software truth for one device: every package with its usage, data consumption, installed versus expected version, and whether it is a system app. Send App Action pushes commands to the selected apps. What it does Per-app table with Send App Action dropdown, Filter dropdown and Search. Columns App Name, Package, App usage, Data usage, Installed vs Expected Version, System App, State. Where to find it Devices → select → Installed Apps

title: App Limits
text: App Limits App limits cap how long an app may run each day. Set a day, an app and a time budget; the platform enforces it and lists the active limits below. Built for shared, classroom and kids devices. What it does Caps daily usage per app — pick Day, App Name, Hour, Minutes, then Submit. Existing limits list below as Day / App Usage. Where to find it Devices → select → App Limits

title: Location trails
text: Location trails Location trails replay where a device has been between two dates. Trails render on map or satellite views with a GPS point list beside them — exportable for records and SLA proof. What it does Plots GPS history between a Start and End date on a Map/Satellite view with a GPS Locations side panel. Pick Start Date → End Date → Submit. Toggle Plot All on Map; Export CSV for records; page with Rows selector. Where to find it Devices → select → Locations

title: Device logs
text: Device logs Logs are the timestamped diary of device and agent events. Filter by type, search the text, refresh for the latest entries — the first stop for “what happened at 2am?” questions. What it does Time-stamped log messages with Search, Type filter (e.g. All Logs) and refresh. Where to find it Devices → select → Logs

title: Applied Restrictions
text: Applied Restrictions Applied restrictions show the effective policy set on this exact unit: type, value and source policy name. When a device behaves unexpectedly, this table names the responsible rule. What it does Searchable table of effective restrictions: Restriction Type, Value, Restriction Name. Use it to confirm a policy reached the unit. Where to find it Devices → select → Applied Restrictions Full catalog: Restrictions →

title: Device Shell
text: Device Shell The shell is a remote terminal into the device for deep diagnosis — battery dumps, package lists, power whitelists — with no site visit. Commands run with the agent’s privileges, so treat access as sensitive. What it does Remote command-line into the device for diagnostics — no site visit. dumpsys battery | grep level pm list packages | grep fieldx Where to find it Devices → select → Device Shell

title: Screen View
text: Screen View Screen view streams the live device screen and forwards taps, swipes and typing as if you held the unit. Unattended access skips on-device acceptance — the feature that makes kiosk and headless fleets supportable. What it does Watch and control the live screen — tap, swipe and type as if holding the device, with unattended access for kiosks. Where to find it Devices → select → Screen View

title: Actions List (15)
text: Actions List (15) Actions are immediate commands executed over the persistent channel — there is no polling delay. Pending marks commands not yet executed. The list spans information, messaging, power, security and maintenance. What it does Pick an action on the left and run it on this device. The Pending badge marks actions not yet executed. Action Effect Refresh Device information Pulls the latest parameters from the unit Send Message Shows a custom message on the device screen Ring / Buzz Device Plays sound to locate a nearby unit Reboot Device Restarts the device remotely Unlock Device Releases the screen lock Lock Device Applies the screen lock immediately Set Device Lease Expiry Sets the rental/lease end date for the unit Clear Failed Downloads Queue Drops stuck app/OTA downloads so they retry cleanly Trigger Collect Logs Pulls diagnostic logs from the device Uninstall an App Removes the specified package from the device Change Device Passcode Sets a new lock-screen passcode remotely Perform Factory Reset Wipes the device to factory state — irreversible Remove EMM Controls Unenrolls the device from management Send Shell Command Runs a shell command on the device Where to find it Devices → select → Action

title: Send Action + SMS fallback
text: Send Action + SMS fallback Send Action delivers over the data channel; Generate SMS Text compiles the same command as an encrypted text for dead zones, basements and roaming units. Control without data is a FieldX signature. What it does Describe the command in the Description box, add a Parameter, then Send Action over data — or Generate SMS Text to deliver it as an encrypted SMS when the device is offline.

title: Before you start
text: Before you start Confirm with your device provider that QR code provisioning is supported. For a low-resolution camera, use the Simplified QR Code shown at the bottom of the enrollment page.

title: Step 1 — Start the device
text: Step 1 — Start the device Unbox and power on the device. Wait for the initial Welcome screen. Tap the same location on the Welcome screen 6 times quickly.

title: Step 2 — Scan the enrollment QR code
text: Step 2 — Scan the enrollment QR code Position the device to scan the unique system enrollment QR code provided by your IT administrator.

title: Step 3 — Connect to Wi-Fi
text: Step 3 — Connect to Wi-Fi When the setup wizard asks for network configuration, use the following values: Setting Value Metered Detect automatically Proxy None IP Settings Static IP Address Static IP on the same subnet as the router Gateway Your local router/default gateway Network Prefix Length 24 DNS 1 34.226.155.149 DNS 2 34.226.155.149 Privacy Use randomized MAC Send device name to network On (Recommended) Choose a static IP that is on the same subnet as your router and is not already being used by another device. Example: If the current IP is 192.168.1.100 and the gateway is 192.168.1.1 , a possible static IP is 192.168.1.101 , provided it is unused. After entering the network details, select Connect and wait until Wi-Fi shows Connected .

title: Step 4 — Complete provisioning
text: Step 4 — Complete provisioning The setup wizard downloads the FieldX Manager App. Follow the remaining Android setup prompts. Grant the requested permissions to the Manager App. Select Done when the “You're all set!” screen appears.

title: Requirements & factory reset
text: Requirements & factory reset Device runs Android 8.0 or higher and is Android Enterprise ready. Fresh out of the box (no accounts) or factory reset — back up data first, reset wipes it.

title: Find the enrollment QR code
text: Find the enrollment QR code 1. Login to the FieldX Web Portal → Downloads page → QR Code Provisioning tab. 2. If the code will not scan, use the Simplified QR Code just below it.

title: After scanning
text: After scanning 1. Accept & Continue → follow setup → grant the Manager app its permissions. 2. If Google Protect warns during install, choose Install Anyway. 3. The device appears under New Devices — tag it and move it to its zone. 4. Next: apply Restrictions and push Apps to it.

title: How to use the Simplified QR Code
text: How to use the Simplified QR Code ⌃ 1. Scan the Simplified QR Code shown on the FieldX enrollment page. 2. Wait for the FieldX Manager App to download and install. 3. The Manager App asks you to scan an Activation QR Code or enter an Access Code. 4. Open Activation QR Code in the FieldX Admin Portal. 5. Use the corresponding activation details to register the device.

title: Find your activation details
text: Find your activation details ⌃ Open Enrol Devices → Activation QR Code in the FieldX Admin Portal. The page provides the information required to register a device, including: Organization Code Access Code Activation QR Code

title: Enroll a device to your organization
text: Enroll a device to your organization 1. Open the FieldX Android application. 2. Select Enroll Device . 3. Scan the Activation QR Code or enter the Access Code manually. 4. Complete the enrollment steps shown on the device.

title: When is Server URL required?
text: When is Server URL required? The Server URL field is required only when connecting to a privately hosted MDM server.

title: What you need
text: What you need ⌃ Android device that is new or factory-reset. USB cable. Recommended: Linux or Mac with the latest Chrome browser. Windows may require additional device drivers depending on the phone model.

title: Step 1 — Prepare the Android device
text: Step 1 — Prepare the Android device 1. Unbox a new device or factory reset an existing device. 2. Power on the device. 3. Complete the Android Setup Wizard. 4. Do not add a Google account. 5. Do not install third-party apps or perform extra setup.

title: Step 2 — Enable USB debugging
text: Step 2 — Enable USB debugging 1. Open Settings → About phone . 2. Tap Build number 7 times. 3. Open Developer options . 4. Turn on USB debugging and confirm the warning.

title: Step 3 — Prepare your computer
text: Step 3 — Prepare your computer Close Android Studio and other tools that use ADB before starting the Web Installer. The Web Installer needs exclusive access to the device. If an ADB server is running, stop it with adb kill-server .

title: Step 4 — Connect and enroll
text: Step 4 — Connect and enroll 1. Connect the Android device to your computer using USB. 2. Connect the device to Wi-Fi. 3. In Web Installer, select Connect your Device . 4. Follow the on-screen provisioning steps. 5. Wait while the FieldX EMM agent is installed and the device is provisioned.

title: Step 5 — Verify enrollment
text: Step 5 — Verify enrollment On the Android device, confirm that the FieldX EMM app/agent is installed. In the FieldX Admin Portal, confirm that the device appears as enrolled and that the required policies and profiles are applied.

title: Requirements
text: Requirements ⌃ Both phones must be connected to the same Wi-Fi network. The target device should be new or freshly factory-reset. The target device should have no Google/user accounts or other device-management app. Wireless debugging must be enabled on the target device. The installer phone needs a FieldX account. The target device should be Android 14 or above.

title: Prepare the target device
text: Prepare the target device 1. Complete the Android setup wizard without signing in to a Google or other account. 2. Open Settings → About phone . 3. Tap Build number 7 times to enable Developer options. 4. Open Settings → System → Developer options . 5. Enable Wireless debugging . 6. Keep the Wireless debugging screen open while pairing.

title: Sign in to FieldX Installer
text: Sign in to FieldX Installer 1. Open FieldX Installer on the installer phone. 2. Enter your FieldX email and password. 3. Tap Sign in . The session may be restored automatically on future launches.

title: Step 1 — Pair the device
text: Step 1 — Pair the device QR pairing 1. On the target: Settings → Developer options → Wireless debugging → Pair device with QR code. 2. On the installer phone, tap Show pairing QR . 3. Scan the QR shown on the installer phone using the target device. Pairing code 1. On the target, choose Pair device with pairing code. 2. On the installer phone, tap Scan for devices . 3. Select the target or enter its IP and pairing port. 4. Enter the 6-digit pairing code and tap Pair .

title: Step 2 — Connect to the device
text: Step 2 — Connect to the device Important: The pairing port and connect port are different. Do not use the pairing port as the connect port. Auto-discover: Select Scan for devices , choose the target, then select Connect when the connection port is available. Manual: Enter the target IP address and the ADB connect port shown under Wireless debugging → IP address & port , then select Connect . When the state shows Connected , select Continue to Provision .

title: Step 3 — Set up the device
text: Step 3 — Set up the device 1. Select Start setup . 2. Wait while provisioning runs. 3. Do not disconnect the device or close FieldX Installer. 4. When complete, the app displays “All done! FieldX is installed and this device is ready to use.” 5. Select Disconnect and check the target device.

title: Before you start
text: Before you start Remove all accounts (Settings → Accounts / Google Accounts) and back up data. Install Platform Tools (Windows/Mac/Linux) and try a spare device first. Copy the Organization code + Access code from the Enrollment Code page.

title: Run the commands
text: Run the commands Download the Manager APK from Plugin Apps, rename to io.fieldx.app.devices-release.apk. Connect with USB debugging on, then run one by one: adb install io.fieldx.app.devices-release.apk adb shell dpm set-device-owner io.fieldx.app.devices/io.droid.admin.DeviceAdminRx adb shell appops set io.fieldx.app.devices GET_USAGE_STATS allow adb shell pm grant io.fieldx.app.devices android.permission.WRITE_SECURE_SETTINGS adb shell dumpsys deviceidle whitelist +io.fieldx.app.devices adb shell cmd notification allow_listener io.fieldx.app.devices/io.fieldx.api.services.NotificationListener adb shell am broadcast --receiver-include-background -a io.app.CONFIGURE --es org ORG_CODE --es access ACCESS_CODE adb reboot If it fails The set-device-owner step must print success — else contact support with the error. After reboot the device appears in the portal within ~10 minutes.

title: Bulk tip: script it
text: Bulk tip: script it Turn the commands into a script and target units with adb -s SERIAL to flash many devices at once.

title: Web Installer does not detect my device
text: Web Installer does not detect my device Usually a host-side connection problem: debugging off, a charge-only cable, missing Windows drivers, or another ADB tool holding the device. Confirm USB debugging is enabled. Try another USB cable or USB port. On Windows, make sure the correct device drivers are installed. Close Android Studio and other ADB tools. If required, run adb kill-server , reconnect the device, and retry.

title: FieldX Installer cannot find my device
text: FieldX Installer cannot find my device Almost always discovery: the two phones are on different networks (or bands), wireless debugging is off, or the pairing screen timed out. Make sure both phones are connected to the same Wi-Fi network. Confirm Wireless debugging is enabled on the target device. For pairing-code mode, keep the target's pairing screen open.

title: Wireless ADB disconnects during setup
text: Wireless ADB disconnects during setup Wireless ADB drops on sleep, network switches, or pairing expiry. Reconnecting and restarting setup resumes cleanly — nothing is half-applied. Return to the Connect step. Reconnect the target device. Return to Set up device. Select Start setup again.

title: Setup says the device is not ready
text: Setup says the device is not ready The agent refuses mixed state: leftover accounts or another management app block device-owner provisioning by Android design. Make sure the target device has no signed-in accounts. Make sure no other device-management app is installed. If necessary, factory reset the device and repeat the preparation steps.

title: Does FieldX support custom OS and firmware?
text: Does FieldX support custom OS and firmware? Answer Yes — stock + custom Android + select Linux, with OEM firmware-team support.

title: Which devices and operating systems are covered?
text: Which devices and operating systems are covered? Answer Android 5–15 + custom builds + Linux IoT + Apple. Legacy + modern.

title: Does it handle OTA firmware updates?

title: Can it run digital signage?
text: Can it run digital signage? Answer Yes — kiosk lock, unattended access, downtime and network SLA monitoring.

text: Is it usable by non-technical teams? Answer Yes — dashboards + automation, and hierarchical access hides complexity.

text: Does it work without Google services? Answer Yes — no Play Store or Firebase required, including regions where Google is blocked.

title: How do devices get enrolled?
text: How do devices get enrolled? Answer Over QR code, web installer, another phone, manual ADB, or pre-installed images — about three minutes per unit. Start at Enroll Device →

title: Which platforms are supported?
text: Which platforms are supported? Answer Android 5–15 (stock, Knox and custom builds), select Linux hardware, and Apple phones, tablets and Macs.

title: What is kiosk mode?
text: What is kiosk mode? Answer Locking a device to one app (POS, signage) or a small approved set (classrooms, carts), enabled and exited remotely with a PIN.

title: How are apps deployed?
text: How are apps deployed? Answer Silently pushed by group with staged rollouts, offered through a private store, or approved from Managed Google Play. See Apps →

title: What happens with no data connection?
text: What happens with no data connection? Answer Encrypted SMS commands still lock, wipe, reboot and sync, and queued installs land on reconnect. See Devices →

title: How are fleets organized?
text: How are fleets organized? Answer Devices collect into groups (bulk policies and apps) inside zones (site isolation with delegated admins). See Groups →

title: Staged rollouts
text: Staged rollouts Rollouts move in stages instead of all at once: prove the build on a small slice, then expand to the fleet. Each device reports its own stage — downloaded, installing, failed or rolled back — so a bad build is visible before it spreads.

title: The Updater agent
text: The Updater agent The Updater agent enforces firmware decisions on the device, pulling builds over CDN and installing them locally. Grab it from console Downloads alongside DeviceManager.apk and fieldx_settings.json. Where to find it Console Downloads

title: Rollback
text: Rollback Updates that fail don't strand devices: failed units roll back and report the rolled-back stage in the OTA report, ready for a fixed build. Check the failure stage first — downloads, installation and device-side blocks fail for different reasons.

title: The OTA report
text: The OTA report The OTA report is the rollout dashboard: every device sits in exactly one stage — downloaded, installing, failed or rolled back. Filter by group or zone to see where an update is stuck, then export for the record. Where to find it Reports → OTA report → filter → Export

title: Stuck downloads
text: Stuck downloads Interrupted transfers sit in the failed-downloads queue and retry dirty. Clearing the queue drops the stuck app and OTA downloads so they retry cleanly — the first fix to try before investigating further. Where to find it Devices → select → Action → Clear Failed Downloads Queue

title: Create account
text: Create account Your account lives on the FieldX console — the web portal where every fleet action happens. Sign up, verify, log in: the dashboard you land on is the same surface you will operate daily. 1. Go to admin.fieldx.io/accounts/register → Sign Up. 2. Verify email → Login at admin.fieldx.io/users/login . 3. You land on the FieldX Console (dashboard with fleet health, compliance, zones).

title: Console tour
text: Console tour The console mirrors the fleet’s structure: health up top, inventory and grouping in the middle, policies-apps-kiosk-OTA as the levers, reports and downloads as the outputs. Learn this map once and every guide below makes sense. Area Use Dashboard Live fleet status, online/offline, compliance donut, recent alerts Devices / Inventory Search, filter, drill into 100+ params per device Buckets & Zones Logical grouping by location/dept/project (isolated policies) Users & Roles Hierarchical access — each user sees only their devices Policies / Apps / Kiosk / OTA Push configs, apps, lockdowns, firmware Reports & Alerts Exports (CSV/Excel), scheduled reports Downloads DeviceManager.apk, Updater.apk, fieldx_settings.json Where to find it Console sidebar after login Console dashboard — fleet health, OS mix and live locations.

title: First device (fastest path — QR)
text: First device (fastest path — QR) The first device proves the whole pipeline — console entry, QR code, agent install, policy download — in about three minutes. Everything after it is the same flow at scale. 1. Console → Devices → Add → QR Enrollment → download/print QR. 2. Factory-reset Android → tap 6x on welcome → scan QR. 3. Device auto-downloads agent + policies + apps. Done in ~3 min. Need another way to enroll? See Enroll Device →

title: Requirements
text: Requirements FieldX is built for constrained environments: decade-old Android versions, de-Googled builds, offline sites with SMS fallback. If the hardware runs Android 5 or better and you have a browser, you can start. Platforms Android 5–15 (stock, Knox, or custom AOSP), select Linux builds, Apple (iOS/iPadOS/macOS). Google Works without Google Play / Firebase — ideal for custom builds & restricted regions. Connectivity Internet preferred, but encrypted SMS fallback keeps control offline. Browser Chrome / Edge / Firefox / Safari. Private-cloud / on-premise available on request.

title: Next steps
text: Next steps One enrolled device turns reading into operating. Bulk enrollment repeats the QR flow across hundreds of units; the Devices inventory is where you will spend most days. Continue with Enroll Device → Or explore Devices →

title: What groups are for
text: What groups are for Definition A group is a logical classification of managed devices — by Department, Branch, Type of use, or Hardware characteristics (e.g. Production Devices, Beta Devices, Internal Test Users, Samsung Devices, TV Boxes). Grouping lets admins manage devices at scale. Use cases Selectively push Apps, apply Restrictions, or push OTA firmware to one group of devices. Groups vs Zones Groups are for managing devices; Zones are for putting devices into different buckets.

title: Three ways to fill a group
text: Three ways to fill a group Groups fill three ways, often combined: hand-picked assignment for precision, bulk lists for migrations, and automatic rules for everything that keeps arriving. Manual addition — pick devices and assign them. Bulk addition — paste IMEI/Serial lists. Automatic grouping — rules place devices themselves.

title: Groups table
text: Groups table The groups table is the starting point for fleet organization: every group with its freshness, member count and attached policies and apps. Row actions run commands on the whole group or delete it. What it does Lists all groups with columns for Name, Last Updated Time, Devices, Restrictions and Apps, plus a Search box and an add (+) button. Row actions Send Action runs a command on the group; Delete removes it. Where to find it Groups (top-level console page) Groups table — every group with devices, policies, apps and row actions.

title: Create Group dialog
text: Create Group dialog Creating a group takes a name, an optional device cap, an optional reported-since cutoff, and an optional Android-Enterprise-only flag — then auto-grouping rules that fill it. One dialog defines both the container and its membership logic. Group Details Group Name (required), Max. Devices (leave empty for unlimited), Apply Auto Rules only to devices Reported Since (date), and Auto add only Android Enterprise Devices checkbox. Auto Grouping Rules Pick a Rule, enter a Value or Regex, then Add — matching devices join automatically. The dialog lets IT admins combine rules and cap group size per requirement. Fill Group Name → set limits → add rules → Add. Cancel discards everything. Create Group dialog — details, limits and auto-grouping rules.

title: Edit group & rules
text: Edit group & rules A group’s rules are living filters: every enrolled device is checked immediately, and every new device is evaluated on arrival. Tighten or loosen the rules and membership follows without manual moves. What it does Change the Group Name, Max. Devices, Reported-Since date or AE-only flag, then Save . Delete (or the ⋮ menu) removes the group. Rule types Manufacturer & Model (e.g. Google, Pixel 7a), Regex on IMEI, Serial or MAC address, and App package (e.g. com.android.vending groups devices with Play Store installed). Matching All rules work on OR basis — a device joins if any one rule matches. Rules apply immediately to enrolled devices and are evaluated for every new device. Tips Use Manufacturer & Model to blacklist manufacturer-bundled apps; Serial mapping for manufacturer batches; IMEI patterns for batch purchases with similar IMEIs; app matching for fleets with different preinstalled apps. Existing rules Listed as Rule Name / Rule Value rows; add more with Rule + Value or Regex + Add. Where to find it Groups → click a group name → Group Details

title: Manual assignment
text: Manual assignment Manual assignment is the precision tool — one or a few devices placed exactly where they belong, whether from the fleet list or from inside a device’s own page. 1. Open My Devices or New Devices (or the top-bar Search), select one or more devices. 2. Click Assign Group on the right side → pick the group → save. 3. From a Device Details page: search by IMEI/Serial → Device ID link → Assign Group → save. Apps and restrictions can take 15–30 minutes to land after assignment.

title: Bulk Assign / Delete Devices
text: Bulk Assign / Delete Devices Bulk membership trades clicks for lists: paste identifiers once instead of ticking hundreds of rows. Built for migrations, batch rollouts and decom fleets. What it does Paste comma-separated IMEI or Serial numbers (pick which with the radio buttons) and Submit — to add units in bulk, or remove them in bulk. Note Removing devices from a group never removes their restrictions or apps. Choose IMEI Number or Serial Number → paste list → Submit.

title: Pro tips
text: Pro tips Name groups technically — by model, make, manufacturer. Auto rules trigger full workflows: grouping auto-pushes apps and restrictions. Deleting devices from a group removes membership only — restrictions and apps stay on.

title: Group devices
text: Group devices The Devices tab answers “who is in this group?” — members with freshness and hardware, plus group-scoped Send, Assign, Remove and Export. Pagination keeps thousand-device groups usable. Toolbar Send Action , Assign Group , Remove Group , Export CSV and a Search-device box. Columns Device ID, IMEI Number, Serial Number, Zone, Device User, Alias, Last Seen Time, Model — with Total rows and Rows-per-page pagination. Where to find it Groups → click a group name → Devices

title: Group restrictions
text: Group restrictions The Restrictions tab shows which policies ride with the group and their Order — the priority ladder that decides which rule wins when policies overlap. What it does Lists attached restriction policies as Name / Order rows — Order is the priority: higher-priority policies win on the same devices. Where to find it Groups → click a group name → Restrictions Full catalog: Restrictions →

title: Group apps
text: Group apps The Apps tab shows which apps the group carries, their versions against expected versions, and per-row Download and Shell shortcuts for direct handling. Columns App Status (e.g. Enabled), Name, Version, Package Name, Last Updated Time — plus per-row Download and Shell cmd shortcuts. Where to find it Groups → click a group name → Apps App lifecycle: Apps →

title: Restrictions — full reference
text: Restrictions — full reference Restrictions are lockdown policies pushed from the console to devices. Each restriction controls one behavior — installing apps, using the camera, joining Wi-Fi — with a priority order that decides which rule wins. Policies attach to groups, so different fleets get different rules.

title: Enroll Device
text: Enroll Device Enrollment is how a device joins FieldX management. Each device is enrolled once — via QR code, web installer, another phone, or activation code — after which it downloads its policies and apps automatically.

title: Devices
text: Devices Devices is the live inventory of every enrolled endpoint. Each device reports 100+ parameters — battery, storage, signal, location — and accepts 20+ instant actions like reboot, lock, wipe, or block. It is where daily fleet control happens.

title: Groups
text: Groups Groups organize devices so policies apply in bulk instead of per device. Smart groups collect devices by department, location, or tags, while buckets and zones isolate sites with their own admins. Policies attach to groups with a priority order that decides which rule wins.

title: Apps
text: Apps Apps management controls which applications exist on devices. Admins silently install, update, or remove apps, block distracting ones through blacklist and whitelist policies, and offer approved tools through a private store that needs no Google Play.

title: Firmware
text: Firmware Firmware management keeps every device on the right software. Updates roll out in stages over CDN with rollback for failures, enforced locally by the Updater agent and tracked per device in the OTA report.

title: Android Enterprise
text: Android Enterprise Android Enterprise is Google's enterprise framework inside FieldX. Work profiles cover BYOD, full management covers corporate units, and Managed Play curates apps — orange pills mark every restriction that needs it.

title: Reports
text: Reports Reports turn fleet data into visibility. Standard reports cover inventory, compliance, apps, OTA, and uptime, exportable as CSV, Excel, or PDF. Alerts notify admins of offline, geofence, or battery events by email, SMS, or webhook.

title: Global Restriction
text: Global Restriction What it is The default restriction of order one, created by the system. It applies to all devices, cannot be deleted, but can be edited by authorized users. Use it for The common set for every device — e.g. disable factory reset, enable auto date & time. Anything group-specific overrides it by higher order. Example: globally disable debugging for all devices, then add a higher-order restriction enabling it for one group — that group gets debugging, the rest do not.

title: Adding a restriction
text: Adding a restriction 1. Side menu → Restrictions → Add at the top of the page. 2. Restriction Name — user-friendly, describing its purpose or group. 3. Order — unique number; lower orders are overridden by higher ones. 4. Group Selection — one or multiple groups from the dropdown. 5. Pick a category and configure each restriction (dropdown or text entry per its description). 6. Add (top-right) to save.

title: Deleting a restriction
text: Deleting a restriction Read first Deleting removes the restriction from the portal but does NOT undo settings already on devices. To lift settings, edit first and set everything to ‘Do not Apply’. Side menu → Restrictions → pick the restriction → Delete → confirm (irreversible). The Global Restriction cannot be deleted — only edited. Deletions are logged in user audit records, so admins can see who removed what.

title: Watchdog setup
text: Watchdog setup Prerequisite Watchdog works only if FieldX is installed as a system app. On capable devices, contact support for know-how. 1. Restrictions page → add or edit the restriction. 2. App Restrictions category → scroll to App Watchdog settings → Add/Update. 3. Enter each app's fully qualified class name (wrong names fail silently) → Submit. 4. Save Changes on top to apply everything.

title: Allow Installing or Sideloading Apps
text: Allow Installing or Sideloading Apps What it does Controls whether the user can install apps from any source at all, including the Play Store. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Where to find it Restrictions / App Installation & Permissions / Disallow App Installs from all Sources When should I use this? Use this for the strictest lockdown, when devices should never gain new apps through user action — for example, single-purpose kiosk hardware. Important notes Note: The FieldX source describes this restriction only as "controls whether the user is allowed to install from all apps," which reads as a typo. The scope above ("any source at all") is inferred from the restriction's name and its position as the broadest of the three install-source restrictions in this section — confirm against your FieldX console before relying on it.

title: Allow App Installs from Unknown Sources
text: Allow App Installs from Unknown Sources What it does Controls whether the user can enable the "Unknown Sources" setting that permits installing apps from outside the Play Store. adb and trusted app stores are not affected by this setting. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Where to find it Restrictions / App Installation & Permissions / Disallow App Installs from Sources except Google Play Store, adb & MDM When should I use this? Use this when devices should only receive apps from the Play Store, adb, or MDM push, while still allowing normal Play Store use.

title: Allow App Installs Unknown Sources Globally
text: Allow App Installs Unknown Sources Globally What it does Disables installs from every unknown source — including adb, third-party app stores, and the Downloads folder — leaving only MDM-pushed installs available. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Where to find it Restrictions / App Installation & Permissions / Disallow App Installs Unknown Sources Globally (except MDM) When should I use this? Use this when even adb-based installs are a risk you want to close off, and MDM push should be the only install path. Important notes Note: This is the narrowest of the three install-source restrictions: it blocks adb as well, which the "except Google Play Store, adb & MDM" restriction above does not.

title: Auto Grant Runtime Permissions to Apps
text: Auto Grant Runtime Permissions to Apps What it does Apps listed here automatically receive all their requested runtime permissions (Location, Storage, Microphone, Camera, Read SMS, etc.) without prompting the user. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of the application(s) that should receive automatic runtime permissions. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Installation & Permissions / Auto Grant Runtime Permissions to Apps When should I use this? Use this for trusted line-of-business apps where a permission prompt would block unattended or kiosk-style operation.

title: Allow user to uninstall apps
text: Allow user to uninstall apps What it does Controls whether the user can uninstall applications from the device. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Allow user to uninstall apps When should I use this? Use this to stop end users from removing required line-of-business or security apps.

title: Allow user to clear App Cache and Storage
text: Allow user to clear App Cache and Storage What it does Controls whether the user can modify installed applications' data through Settings or the launcher, such as clearing cache or storage. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Allow user to clear App Cache and Storage When should I use this? Use this when clearing app data could disrupt a workflow that depends on cached or local app state.

title: Blacklist Apps
text: Blacklist Apps What it does Hides the listed apps on the device without uninstalling them. Removing an app from this list does not re-enable it — it must be explicitly added to the Whitelist. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of the application(s) to hide. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Blacklist Apps When should I use this? Use this to hide distracting or non-business apps (games, social media) without removing them from the device.

title: Whitelist Apps
text: Whitelist Apps What it does Reverses a previous Blacklist entry for the listed apps. This restriction only undoes blacklisting — it has no other effect. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of the application(s) to re-enable. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Whitelist Apps When should I use this? Use this to restore visibility of an app that was previously hidden by the Blacklist Apps restriction.

title: Disable Apps from Uninstall
text: Disable Apps from Uninstall What it does Prevents the user from uninstalling the listed apps. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of the application(s) to protect from uninstall. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Disable Apps from Uninstall When should I use this? Use this to protect specific required apps from removal without blocking uninstalls device-wide.

title: Enable Apps for Uninstall
text: Enable Apps for Uninstall What it does Reverses a previous "Disable Apps from Uninstall" entry, allowing the listed apps to be uninstalled again. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of the application(s) to re-allow uninstalling. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Enable Apps for Uninstall When should I use this? Use this to restore the ability to uninstall an app that was previously protected.

title: Uninstall Listed Apps from Device
text: Uninstall Listed Apps from Device What it does Force-uninstalls the listed apps if they are currently installed. If a system app is listed, it is disabled instead, since system apps cannot be uninstalled. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of the application(s) to remove. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Uninstall Listed Apps from Device When should I use this? Use this to clean unwanted or non-compliant apps off devices that already have them installed.

title: Permitted Apps on Device
text: Permitted Apps on Device What it does Restricts the device to only the apps on this list. Every other app — including sideloaded ones — is automatically uninstalled or disabled. What to enter Enter the package name(s) of every application that should remain permitted on the device. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Permitted Apps Policy When should I use this? Use this for locked-down, single-purpose deployments where only an approved app set should ever run. Important notes Note: This is an allowlist model: anything not listed is treated as non-permitted. Pair it with "Non-Permitted App Action" below to control what happens to those apps.

title: Action for Unauthorized App installs
text: Action for Unauthorized App installs What it does Chooses how the device handles an app that isn't on the Permitted Apps Policy list. Option What it does No Action The app is left alone. Uninstall immediately The app is force-uninstalled if it is a user-installed app. Hide them from Apps list The app is hidden from the launcher without being removed. This is the default. Disable the App The app is disabled and cannot be launched. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / App Management & Control / Non-Permitted App Action When should I use this? Use this together with the Permitted Apps Policy to decide how strictly non-approved apps are dealt with — from a soft hide up to a hard uninstall.

title: Unified Password
text: Unified Password What it does Controls whether the managed profile is allowed to share a single lock-screen challenge with the primary user, rather than requiring its own. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Minimum Android API level Pie 9.0 (28) Where to find it Restrictions / Password & Lock Screen / Unified Password When should I use this? Use this when the managed (work) profile should require its own separate lock-screen credential from the personal profile.

title: Max. Failed Password Attempts
text: Max. Failed Password Attempts What it does Sets the number of failed lock-screen attempts allowed before the device is automatically wiped and its data deleted. What to enter Enter the maximum number of failed attempts to allow before a wipe is triggered. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Password & Lock Screen / Max. Failed Password Attempts When should I use this? Use this to protect data on lost or stolen devices — set conservatively, since this triggers a full wipe.

title: Allow Lock Screen
text: Allow Lock Screen What it does Controls whether the user is permitted to set a Keyguard (lock screen) at all. Disallowing this removes the user's ability to set one. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Password & Lock Screen / Allow Lock Screen When should I use this? Use this only in specific shared-device or kiosk scenarios where a lock screen would get in the way of the intended use.

title: Keyguard Password Security
text: Keyguard Password Security What it does Sets the minimum lock-screen password complexity required on the device. Option What it does High Security Requires the high-security lock-screen password policy. Medium Security Applies the medium-security lock-screen password policy. Recommended for most deployments. Low Security Applies the low-security lock-screen password policy. Any Password Security Allows any of the supported password-security levels. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Password & Lock Screen / Keyguard Password Security When should I use this? Use this to enforce a minimum password strength across managed devices.

title: Keyguard Timeout
text: Keyguard Timeout What it does Sets how long a passcode can go unchanged before the user is forced to reset it. Option What it does 10 days The user must reset their passcode every 10 days. 20 days The user must reset their passcode every 20 days. 30 days The user must reset their passcode every 30 days. Never The passcode never expires. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Password & Lock Screen / Lock Screen Timeout When should I use this? Use this to enforce periodic passcode rotation as part of a security policy.

title: Lock Screen Message
text: Lock Screen Message What it does Sets device-owner information shown on the lock screen. This overrides any owner information the user set manually and prevents the user from changing it further. What to enter Enter the message to display on the lock screen. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Password & Lock Screen / Lock Screen Message When should I use this? Use this to display organization contact or ownership information for anyone who finds a lost device.

title: User Switch
text: User Switch What it does Controls whether switching to a different user is blocked from the current user. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / User Switch When should I use this? Use this on shared or single-assignee devices where other user profiles should not be reachable.

title: Allow add Managed Profile
text: Allow add Managed Profile What it does Controls whether the user can add a managed (work) profile to the device. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Allow add Managed Profile When should I use this? Use this to control whether users can create their own managed profile outside of MDM provisioning.

title: Add User
text: Add User What it does Controls whether the user can add new users to the device. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Add User When should I use this? Use this to prevent uncontrolled proliferation of user accounts on managed hardware.

title: Remove Managed Profile
text: Remove Managed Profile What it does Controls whether the managed profile can be removed by someone other than its profile owner. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Remove Managed Profile When should I use this? Use this to stop the managed profile (and its enrollment) from being deleted outside of MDM control.

title: Remove User
text: Remove User What it does When set on the primary user, controls whether that user can remove other users from the device. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Remove User When should I use this? Use this to prevent the primary user from deleting other user accounts on a shared device.

title: Allow Change User Icon
text: Allow Change User Icon What it does Controls whether the user is allowed to change their user icon. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Minimum Android API level Nougat 7.0 (24) Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Allow Change User Icon When should I use this? Use this for cosmetic lockdown on shared or kiosk devices.

title: Share Into Managed Profile
text: Share Into Managed Profile What it does Controls whether the user can share files, pictures, or data from the primary profile into the managed profile — either by sending it directly or by picking it up from within an app in the managed profile. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Minimum Android API level Pie 9.0 (28) Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Share Into Managed Profile When should I use this? Use this to control one-way data flow from the personal side into the work profile.

title: Modify Accounts
text: Modify Accounts What it does Controls whether the user can add or remove accounts, unless those accounts are added programmatically by an Authenticator. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Minimum Android API level Jelly Bean 4.3 (18) Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Modify Accounts When should I use this? Use this to stop users from adding personal accounts (email, cloud storage, etc.) to a managed device.

title: Cross Profile Copy Paste
text: Cross Profile Copy Paste What it does Controls whether clipboard content can be pasted into a different user or profile than the one it was copied from. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Minimum Android API level Lollipop 5.0 (21) Where to find it Restrictions / Multi-User & Account Management / Cross Profile Copy Paste When should I use this? Use this to prevent data from the work profile being pasted into personal apps, or vice versa.

title: Factory Reset
text: Factory Reset What it does Controls whether the user can perform a factory reset from Settings. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM, Android Enterprise Minimum Android API level Lollipop 5.0 (21) Where to find it Restrictions / Device Reset & Boot Security / Factory Reset When should I use this? Use this to stop a user from wiping enrollment and data by resetting the device themselves.

title: Hard Reset
text: Hard Reset What it does Controls whether the user can perform a hard reset using Download mode. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for Not specified in the FieldX source. Where to find it Restrictions / Device Reset & Boot Security / Hard Reset When should I use this? Use this alongside Factory Reset to close the lower-level reset path as well.

title: Safe Boot
text: Safe Boot What it does Controls whether the user is allowed to reboot the device into Safe Mode. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for FieldX EMM Minimum Android API level Marshmallow 6.0 (23) Where to find it Restrictions / Device Reset & Boot Security / Safe Boot When should I use this? Use this to stop users from bypassing device-owner apps by booting into Safe Mode, where third-party apps don't run.

title: OEM Unlock
text: OEM Unlock What it does Controls whether the user is allowed to unlock the bootloader. Option What it does Allow Allows the behavior controlled by this restriction. Disallow Prevents the behavior controlled by this restriction. Available for Not specified in the FieldX source. Where to find it Restrictions / Device Reset & Boot Security / OEM Unlock When should I use this? Use this to prevent bootloader unlocking, which could otherwise be used to bypass device management entirely.

title: Google Factory Reset Protection ID
text: Google Factory Reset Protection ID What it does Sets the comma-separated Google Account ID(s) used for Factory Reset Protection (FRP). title: Standard reports
text: Standard reports Standard reports are the five ready-made lenses on a fleet. Each one filters by group, zone, status or time range, so the same report serves a technician checking ten units and an auditor reviewing ten thousand. Report Shows Answers Inventory Hardware and software per device: model, OS, apps, memory, ownership What do we own, and how old is it? Compliance Policy adherence and violations fleet-wide, with per-device drill-down Which units break the rules? App Install state and versions, pivoted by device or by app Did the rollout actually land? OTA Firmware rollout stages: downloaded, installing, failed, rolled back Where is the update stuck? Data usage / SLA Consumption per device and signage uptime percentages Can we prove the SLA? Where to find it Reports → pick type → filter → Export (CSV/Excel/PDF)

title: Alerts
text: Alerts Alerts watch thresholds so humans don’t have to. Instead of patrolling dashboards, admins define what counts as trouble once — then get told the moment it happens, on the channel that reaches them. Trigger Example Offline Device silent for longer than the grace period Geofence exit Delivery unit leaves its assigned zone Low battery Kiosk drops below the charge threshold mid-shift Non-compliance Unit drifts out of its assigned policies Channels Email for records, SMS for urgency, webhook for piping into ticketing or dashboards. Assignment Rules attach to zones or groups, so store managers hear about their stores — not the whole fleet. Where to find it Alerts → Rule → Channel → Assign

title: Scheduled reports
text: Scheduled reports Scheduled reports run themselves: pick a report, its filters and recipients once, and it arrives by email on cadence — daily health digests, weekly compliance packs, monthly SLA evidence. Automation replaces the Monday-morning export ritual and guarantees the audit trail exists before anyone asks for it. Where to find it Reports → pick type → Schedule → recipients → cadence

title: Export formats
text: Export formats Every report exports three ways. CSV feeds spreadsheets and scripts, Excel arrives formatted for sharing with non-technical readers, and PDF freezes a timestamped snapshot for compliance files. Exports honor the active filters, so what you see is what leaves the building.

title: Retention & delivery
text: Retention & delivery Retention decides how far back you can investigate; delivery decides how reports reach you. Short history with manual exports suits daily ops and keeps storage lean. Standard plans keep 60-day device history; extended plans add unlimited history, scheduled email and custom BI export for ERP and analytics tooling.

title: Apps Daily Usage Limits
text: Apps Daily Usage Limits What it does Sets daily usage limits for individual apps, to manage screen time more effectively. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Device Usage Limits / Apps Daily Usage Limits When should I use this? Use this to cap time spent in specific apps, such as games or social media, on managed devices.

title: Daily Device Cut-off Time
text: Daily Device Cut-off Time What it does Sets a daily time after which the device cannot be used, except for designated emergency apps, which remain available throughout. What to enter Enter the daily cut-off time. Available for FieldX EMM Where to find it Restrictions / Device Usage Limits / Daily Device Cut-off Time When should I use this? Use this to enforce device-free hours, for example overnight on employee- or student-assigned devices.

title: Total Screen Time for the day (in Hours)
text: Total Screen Time for the day (in Hours) What it does Sets a total daily screen-time budget.
